1	/**
2	 * Whole calendar days between two `YYYY-MM-DD` keys.
3	 *
4	 * Built from the date parts via `Date.UTC` rather than parsing the strings as
5	 * local timestamps: `worn_on` is a DATE in the user's local calendar, and
6	 * subtracting two local timestamps across a DST change yields 23 or 25 hours,
7	 * which rounds to the wrong number of days.
8	 *
9	 * Shared by the item-detail tiles ("14 days ago") and the stats screen's
10	 * gathering-dust list. It was written once for the former and must not be
11	 * written a second time for the latter — the DST care above is exactly the kind
12	 * of detail a re-implementation loses.
13	 */
14	export function daysBetween(from: string, to: string): number {
15	  const a = Date.UTC(+from.slice(0, 4), +from.slice(5, 7) - 1, +from.slice(8, 10));
16	  const b = Date.UTC(+to.slice(0, 4), +to.slice(5, 7) - 1, +to.slice(8, 10));
17	  return Math.round((b - a) / 86_400_000);
18	}

3	 *
4	 * `en-IE` is the euro locale whose conventions match the rest of the interface;
5	 * the German content the spec plans will want `de-DE` here. One hard-coded

7	 *
8	 * Lives here rather than in `lib/closet/wear-stats.ts` because two screens now

10	 * `Intl.NumberFormat` declarations are two places for the currency to drift.
11	 * The design prices Pro at £5; the app is EU-region and every other price
12	 * renders in euro, so the £ was settled as a design-file artefact on 2026-08-05
13	 * (`docs/MONETISATION.md`).
14	 */
15	const MONEY = new Intl.NumberFormat("en-IE", { style: "currency", currency: "EUR" });
16	
17	export function formatMoney(amount: number): string {
18	  return MONEY.format(amount);
19	}

1	import { formatMoney } from "@/lib/format/money";
2	import { daysBetween } from "@/lib/format/days";
3	
4	/**
5	 * The aggregates behind `/stats` (Fitcheck.dc.html:737-780).
6	 *
7	 * Pure functions over rows the caller has already fetched — no Supabase here,
8	 * so every number on that screen is testable without a database. There is no AI
9	 * call anywhere on this screen, including the gap analysis (see ./gap.ts).
10	 */
11	
12	type PricedItem = { id: string; price: number | null };
13	
14	/**
15	 * `price` is nullable and most closets are mostly null: the tagger cannot read
16	 * a price off a photograph, so it is only ever there because the user typed it.
17	 * Every total therefore has to mean "of the pieces we know about", and the
18	 * screen has to be honest that it is not the whole wardrobe.
19	 */
20	export function closetStats(
21	  items: PricedItem[],
22	  logs: { item_id: string }[],
23	): { value: string; totalWears: number; avgCostPerWear: string | null } {
24	  const total = items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + (i.price ?? 0), 0);
25	  const totalWears = logs.length;
26	  return {
27	    value: formatMoney(total),
28	    totalWears,
29	    // Null rather than 0 or "€0.00" on either empty branch. Dividing by zero
30	    // wears prints €Infinity, and €0.00 for an unpriced closet states something
31	    // false — the UI hides the tile instead. Same stance as `itemWearStats`.
32	    avgCostPerWear: totalWears > 0 && total > 0 ? formatMoney(total / totalWears) : null,
33	  };
34	}
35	
36	/** The n most-worn item ids, highest first. Pieces with no wears are excluded. */
37	export function mostWorn(items: PricedItem[], wearsById: Record<string, number>, n: number): string[] {
38	  return items
39	    .map((i) => ({ id: i.id, wears: wearsById[i.id] ?? 0 }))
40	    .filter((i) => i.wears > 0)
41	    .sort((a, b) => b.wears - a.wears)
42	    .slice(0, n)
43	    .map((i) => i.id);
44	}
45	
46	/**
47	 * The n longest-idle pieces, with how many days it has been.
48	 *
49	 * A never-worn item is the whole point of the section, not a gap in the data —
50	 * the pieces you never reach for are exactly the ones with no wear rows. They
51	 * sort FIRST, above anything merely worn a long time ago, because "you have
52	 * never worn this" is the stronger version of the same statement.
53	 *
54	 * ⚠️ `days` is `null` for those, not `Infinity`. Infinity sorts correctly and
55	 * then reaches the screen as "∞ days ago"; null forces the UI to say "Never
56	 * worn", which is both true and the more damning line.
57	 */
58	export function gatheringDust(
59	  items: PricedItem[],
60	  lastWornById: Record<string, string>,
61	  today: string,
62	  n: number,
63	): { id: string; days: number | null }[] {
64	  return items
65	    .map((i) => {
66	      const last = lastWornById[i.id];
67	      return { id: i.id, days: last ? daysBetween(last, today) : null };
68	    })
69	    .sort((a, b) => (b.days ?? Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY) - (a.days ?? Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY))
70	    .slice(0, n);
71	}

content.text:
I've read every changed file in full. This change is a pure refactor plus new pure helper/aggregation modules:

- `lib/format/days.ts`: extracted date-diff utility over `YYYY-MM-DD` strings from the local DB. No sinks (no shell, SQL, HTTP, filesystem, HTML, eval).
- `lib/format/money.ts`: extracted `Intl.NumberFormat` wrapper. Deterministic pure function; no sinks.
- `lib/stats/aggregate.ts`: pure reducers/sorters over already-fetched rows. No DB, network, filesystem, or rendering; no user-controlled data reaches any dangerous sink; division-by-zero and empty-set edge cases are handled (`totalWears > 0 && total > 0`).
- `lib/closet/wear-stats.ts`: unchanged behavior — swapped local `MONEY`/`daysBetween` for the extracted imports.
- Test file: jest only, no runtime impact.

Cross-cutting checks:
- No new entry points (HTTP handlers, RPC, IPC, webhooks, uploads, CLI).
- No sinks touched (no exec, SQL, template, HTML, deserialization, outbound HTTP, log/telemetry of PII, IAM, IaC).
- No parser/validator differentials — `daysBetween` uses fixed-offset `slice()` on internally-sourced date strings; `Math.round` on a UTC ms diff is the accepted DST-safe idiom.
- No allowlists, permission matchers, gates, or authz logic added/modified.
- No control regression: the deleted `MONEY` / `daysBetween` are re-exported with identical semantics; the diff of the two implementations is byte-identical.
- Sibling parity holds: both callers (`itemWearStats`, `closetStats`) still guard the divisor before division.
- No sensitive-to-observability paths introduced.
